item.text: {"question_id":"8B.10","answer":"By the end of 2023, Tshisekedi’s government had converted parts of its program into formal law, planning frameworks, institutional arrangements, and some observable implementation, but the supplied evidence does not establish broad durable achievement. The record supports formal conversion through the victim-reparation framework, budget-governance rules, the CENAREF/anti-money-laundering framework, continued PDL-145T implementation, free-primary-education implementation with enrollment reaching about four million in 2022, and UN-supported justice staffing and access in 2023 (BATCH-0029-E001; BATCH-0029-E003; BATCH-0019-E003; BATCH-0010-E004; BATCH-0012-R01-E019). These are mainly legal, organizational, planned, or output-level gains; the supplied passages do not demonstrate their persistence, nationwide institutionalization, independent 2023 outcomes, or isolated presidential causation, and several depended materially on UN, donor, or World Bank support. The election occurred on the normal constitutional schedule and Tshisekedi’s coalition won a large legislative majority, but external UN support was important, the process had logistical defects and disputed results, reforms were incompletely implemented, and CENI and the Constitutional Court remained perceived as politicized (BATCH-0010-E005; BATCH-0028-E010; BATCH-0013-E010; BATCH-0028-E018). Major program-relevant failures persisted: the state of siege did not meet its stated security objectives, the EAC regional force produced no substantial progress and withdrew, conflict and displacement intensified, food insecurity remained at crisis levels, and schooling and purchasing-power outcomes remained poor (BATCH-0012-R03-E004; BATCH-0011-E016; BATCH-0013-E014; BATCH-0020-E009; BATCH-0028-E020). The end-period position is therefore mixed: real but incompletely attributable formal conversion and selected implementation coexisted with severe reversals and weakly demonstrated durability.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0029-E001","BATCH-0029-E003","BATCH-0019-E003","BATCH-0010-E004","BATCH-0012-R01-E019","BATCH-0010-E005","BATCH-0028-E010"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0013-E010","BATCH-0028-E018","BATCH-0012-R03-E004","BATCH-0011-E016","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0020-E009","BATCH-0028-E020","BATCH-0014-E003"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The supplied evidence is concentrated on 2023 and cannot establish long-term durability for reforms initiated in 2022 or implemented during 2023.","Positive outcomes are often reported for the government collectively or with substantial external support; ruler-specific causal attribution is therefore limited.","Some outcome evidence covers Tshisekedi’s full 2019–2023 tenure rather than the end of 2023 alone, and does not isolate policy effects from inherited conditions, conflict, or wider shocks."],"corrections_made":["Replaced claims of durable law, institutions, and administrative practice with the narrower supported claim of formal conversion and selected implementation.","Removed the unsupported implication that 2022 education results demonstrated 2023 durability.","Reweighted the election evidence to account for external UN support, logistical defects, disputed legitimacy, and incomplete electoral reform.","Integrated contrary evidence on politicized institutions, nonimplementation, displacement, food insecurity, schooling, purchasing power, and failed security efforts.","Preserved the period as ending in 2023 and retained causal and durability uncertainty."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["A full ledger review would be warranted if additional independent evidence establishes 2023 execution, persistence, financing, or outcomes for the cited legal and institutional reforms.","Further review could clarify the ruler-specific contribution relative to UN, donor, coalition, bureaucratic, military, and inherited-capacity effects."]}
